entries.title: Al-Andalus (Islamic Spain)
entries.summary: Al-Andalus refers to Muslim-ruled territories in the Iberian Peninsula from the 8th century until the fall of Granada in 1492 CE, famed for cities like Cordoba, Seville, and Granada.
entries.detailed_information: Muslim forces crossed into Iberia in 711 CE. An Umayyad emirate, later caliphate, centered on Cordoba became a major cultural capital. After caliphal collapse, taifa kingdoms rose, followed by Almoravid and Almohad interventions from North Africa. The Nasrid Kingdom of Granada was the last Muslim polity, ending in 1492. Al-Andalus is remembered for architecture, learning, poetry, and complex interreligious relations — including coexistence and conflict across centuries.
entries.historical_significance: A major western Islamic civilization linking Maghrib, Europe, and Mediterranean culture.
related_questions: What was the Caliphate of Cordoba?

entries.title: Caliphate of Cordoba
entries.summary: The Caliphate of Cordoba, proclaimed by Abd al-Rahman III in 929 CE, was a high point of Andalusi political power and cultural prestige.
entries.detailed_information: Building on the emirate founded by Abd al-Rahman I (a surviving Umayyad), Abd al-Rahman III declared a caliphate rivaling Abbasids and Fatimids in claim. Cordoba became renowned for libraries, scholarship, and monumental architecture such as the Great Mosque (Mezquita). After 1031, the caliphate fragmented into taifa states.
entries.historical_significance: Symbol of Andalusi golden cultural-political era.
related_questions: Why did Muslim rule in Spain decline?
